items.prompt: A new ticket status "rejected" ships, but nobody touches `getStatusLabel`. A rejected ticket is passed in. What label does the UI show, and why is that a quiet bug rather than a crash?
items.answer: "Archived": no branch matches, so it falls through to the final return and mislabels it silently
distractors: "Unknown": the first guard returns Unknown for any status the function has not seen before
undefined: an if/else-if chain with no matching branch returns nothing, so the label shows up blank
It throws a TypeError: `t.status` is compared against strings that do not include "rejected"
items.explanation: The `if (!t)` guard only catches a missing ticket. Unmatched statuses reach `return "Archived"`; the lesson's own 'Add a rejected case' exercise exists because the fallback hides missing cases.

items.prompt: In the rating recommendation, `rating` is changed from 6.8 to exactly 8. Which string is chosen?
items.answer: "Must watch": the first test uses >=, so 8 satisfies it and the inner ternary is skipped
distractors: "Worth it": 8 is not strictly above the threshold, so it falls into the middle band
"Skip": a nested ternary evaluates its last branch whenever both conditions are true
A SyntaxError: chained ternaries need parentheses wrapped around the inner ternary expression
items.explanation: Ternaries are evaluated left to right; `rating >= 8` is true for 8, so its branch is the value of the whole expression.

items.prompt: `addToWatchlist({ year: 1999 })` is called. What is logged, and what design benefit of the guard clause does this show?
items.answer: Only "Invalid movie": the guard returns early, so the happy path below needs no nesting
distractors: "Added: undefined": the guard only rejects a null movie, not one that lacks a title
Both "Invalid movie" and "Added: undefined": console.log does not stop the function
Nothing: an object without a title is falsy and the function exits silently
items.explanation: `!movie || !movie.title` is true for an object with no title; the bare `return` ends the function. Guard clauses keep the happy path flat.

items.prompt: After `const firstFew = watchlist.slice(0, 2)`, the code runs `firstFew.push("Alien")`. Does `watchlist` gain "Alien"?
items.answer: No: slice returns a new, shallow-copied array, so the push leaves watchlist unchanged
distractors: Yes: slice returns a live, shared view of the array, so writes show up in watchlist
Yes, but only if "Alien" lands in the first two positions: the slice covers just those
No: push on a sliced array throws, as slices are returned as frozen copies
items.explanation: The lesson: `.slice()` returns a shallow copy without mutating. The copy is a separate array; only the element objects (if any) would be shared.

items.prompt: Someone rewrites the loop as `for (let i = 0; i <= watchlist.length; i++) console.log(i, watchlist[i])`. What changes in the output?
items.answer: One extra iteration logs index length with undefined: valid indexes stop at length - 1
distractors: The first element is skipped: a <= condition makes the loop start counting from index 1
It throws a RangeError: reading at the index equal to the array length is out of bounds
Nothing changes: the engine clamps an out-of-range index to the last valid element
items.explanation: Arrays are zero-based; reading one past the end is not an error in JS, it just yields undefined. This is the lesson's off-by-one mistake (`<= length`).

items.prompt: A teammate writes `const labels = movies.forEach(m => m.title)` and then renders `labels.join(", ")`. What happens, and what was the intended method?
items.answer: labels is undefined: join throws a TypeError, and map would return the results
distractors: labels holds the three titles: an arrow with no braces returns its expression to forEach
labels is an empty array: forEach only collects the callback's truthy return values
labels is the original movies array: forEach returns the array it iterated, unchanged
items.explanation: The lesson's first common mistake: forEach returns undefined. Use map to transform.

items.prompt: To build a "seen" shelf, the code calls `movies.find(m => m.watched)`. Two movies are watched. What does the shelf get, and what should have been used?
items.answer: Only The Matrix object: find stops at the first match, while filter returns all watched movies
distractors: An array with The Matrix and Inception: find returns all matches whenever more than one exists
Inception: find scans from the end of the array toward the start and stops at a match
true: find only reports whether any element matched the predicate, like some
items.explanation: find returns one element (or undefined). The lesson warns: using find when you need all matches — use filter.

items.prompt: A logging side effect is added inside the `every(m => m.watched)` callback. For the three sample movies, how many times does the callback run?
items.answer: Twice: The Matrix passes, Dune fails, and every stops without visiting Inception
distractors: Three times: every inspects all elements, in order, before it returns a boolean
Once: every stops after the first element that passes the test and returns true
Zero times until the result is read: every is evaluated lazily on access
items.explanation: every short-circuits on the first false (some short-circuits on the first true) — the lesson's third common mistake.

items.prompt: The total is refactored to `movies.reduce((sum, m) => sum + m.minutes)` with the `, 0` removed (and no filter). What value comes out?
items.answer: A string: the first movie object is the accumulator, giving "[object Object]155148"
distractors: 439: reduce quietly defaults the accumulator to 0 whenever no initial value is given
NaN: the accumulator starts as undefined, and undefined + 155 is not a number
303: the first element is used as the start value, and its own minutes are skipped
items.explanation: Without an initial value, reduce uses element 0 (the whole Matrix object) as the accumulator. The lesson: forgetting the initial value gives the first element as initial — bugs.

items.prompt: In `byRatingBand`, the line is simplified to `acc[band] = acc[band] + 1`. What does the console show?
items.answer: { great: NaN, good: NaN }: each band first reads undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN
distractors: { great: 2, good: 1 }: a missing key reads as 0, so the counts come out right
A TypeError, as you cannot read a property that does not exist yet on acc
{ great: 1, good: 1 }, as each key can only be assigned once inside reduce
items.explanation: `(acc[band] || 0)` supplies the missing starting count; without it the first increment is undefined + 1.

items.prompt: In the event-loop example, the timer is given a delay of 0. In what order do the four logs appear?
items.answer: Synchronous "1" and "4" first, then the promise microtask, and the setTimeout macrotask last
distractors: Exactly in source order: with a zero delay, the timer callback is effectively synchronous
The timeout callback runs before the promise callback, as it was scheduled earlier in the file
"1", then both async callbacks interleaved with "4" depending on CPU load
items.explanation: Synchronous code runs to completion; then the microtask queue (promise reactions) drains before the next macrotask (the timer).

items.prompt: A dashboard calls `safeFetch(url)` and the server answers 500. What does the dashboard receive, and what is the trade-off of this design?
items.answer: An empty array: the status check throws and catch recovers, hiding an outage behind an empty list
distractors: A rejected promise with HTTP 500: the throw inside try escapes, and catch never runs
The parsed 500 error body: fetch resolves on any status and json() still runs
undefined: returning a value from inside a catch block is ignored in an async function
items.explanation: `if (!r.ok) throw` turns an HTTP error into an exception (fetch alone would resolve), and `return []` hides it from callers.

items.prompt: `const a = createCounter(); const b = createCounter(); a(); a();` — what does the next call `b()` return?
items.answer: 1: each createCounter call makes its own count, closed over by that one function
distractors: 3: both counters share the one count variable, which is declared inside createCounter
0: b has not been incremented yet and returns the value from before the ++
NaN: count is reset to undefined once createCounter has finished and returned
items.explanation: Closures remember the lexical environment of the call that created them; separate calls mean separate environments.

items.prompt: Someone deletes `clearTimeout(t)` from `debounce`. The user types "m", "mo", "mov" within 300 ms. What happens now?
items.answer: Three searches fire, each 300 ms after its own call: the earlier pending timers stay scheduled
distractors: One search fires for "mov": t is reassigned, and the earlier timers are discarded automatically
No search fires: calling setTimeout throws while a previous timer is still pending
One search fires for "m": later calls see t already set and skip scheduling
items.explanation: Reassigning t only loses the handle; the earlier timers still run. clearTimeout is what makes only the last call within the window fire.

items.front: A switch on ticket status has `case "open": label = "New";` with no break, followed by `case "in_progress": label = "Being worked on"; break;`. Open tickets show "Being worked on". Why?
items.back: Fallthrough: without break, execution continues into the next case's statements, overwriting the label. Add break (or return) at the end of each case.

items.front: On a 3-item watchlist, `watchlist[99] = "Heat"` runs. What are the length and the contents of the gap?
items.back: length becomes 100 and indexes 3..98 are empty holes (sparse array); loops over length then visit 96 undefined slots.

items.front: `const out = []; movies.map(m => out.push(m.title));` works, but review flags it. What is wrong?
items.back: map is used for a side effect: it builds and discards an array of push return values (lengths). Return the transformed value instead: `const out = movies.map(m => m.title)`.

items.front: In `run()`, `blockScoped` is declared with let inside `if (true) { ... }` and logged after the block closes. What happens, and what would var have done?
items.back: ReferenceError: let/const live only in their block. With var the variable is function-scoped, so the log would print 42 — the leak the lesson calls dangerous.
